Text:
A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What if , whole world’s internet gets shutdown ?
What if Whole world’s internet gets shutdown At once cumulatively for 1 day 1 week 1 month 1 year From any whatever reason



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh man, that would be wild! First off, if it went down for just a day, people might treat it like a weird holiday. Like, no endless scrolling or Zoom meetings, just a forced break. Folks might actually talk to each other face-to-face or maybe they’ll pull out actual books or board games. But a week without it? Yikes. People might start freaking out about bills and work stuff piling up. Also discover all those super dated tv shows they have on DVDs... so it’ll be fine for a second, then weird. For a month, we'd be in a whole new world. Businesses that rely on the internet might struggle to adapt, so it’d be a bit chaotic. Someone should check on all the teens going through TikTok withdrawal. Libraries would be hotspots again, if they're stocked up with relevant info and not just old teen novels. For a whole year, well, I think we’d become more self-sufficient, which is a plus. People would have to innovate big time to keep things running. But dang, imagine explaining the 'before time' internet to kids who don’t remember. Our routines and habits would be totally reshaped. You'd think about cooking, sports, and nature differently, for sure.

I’m working on an AI-powered tool that helps people **turn big goals into manageable steps and stay on track over time**. The idea is to make goal-setting **less overwhelming** and help you adjust as life happens—without needing a coach or mentor. Here’s how it works: ✅ **Creates a step-by-step plan based on your goal** (fitness, business, learning a skill, etc.). ✅ **Tracks your progress & adapts**—if you fall behind, it adjusts instead of just sending annoying reminders. ✅ **Keeps you accountable** with check-ins, progress tracking, and optional small-group support. The goal is to make sure you’re **actually making progress**, not just setting goals and forgetting about them. Would this be useful to you? What’s missing that would make this something you'd actually use?



They receive the following reply to their post:

Would I use an AI to nanny me into finishing a goal? People gotta stop relying on robots for stuff you can do with a pen and paper or, I dunno, your brain! I mean, goals are hard and if you need a machine to keep you accountable, maybe the goal ain't the problem. Maybe you're the problem. Sounds more like a future where we're all just baby adults being herded like sheep by AI. If someone can't remember their own goals, maybe they should stay off the internet for a while and think about what they're doing with their life.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Iwtl how to write better/professionally
I want to learn how to song write and also write novels. However I don’t know where to start or how to learn writing. Thanks in advance !



They receive the following reply to their post:

Hey there! I was in the same boat when I started writing. Let me tell you, one of the things that worked for me was just diving in without worrying too much at first. For songwriting, I started by listening to songs I love and breaking them down. Like, what's the chorus doing? How do the verses lead into it? I tried writing my own lyrics with random ideas and slowly connected them to melodies in my head. Sometimes it was just silly, but it’s all about practice. For novels, reading similar books in your favorite genres really helps. When I decided to attempt my first novel, I started jotting down little snippets of scenes and dialogues in a notebook—nothing too structured at first. You can do it everyday or make it a regular habit. Little by little it turns into something. Online writing communities are amazing too. I joined a couple of them, and the feedback was gold. Sure, my initial drafts were sometimes brutalized, but I learned so much! Also, don’t stress too much about being “professional” right out the gate. Focus on getting comfortable with expressing your thoughts. Maybe get a recent song you love, grab a cup of coffee and try to write something in a style similar to it. Or grab a favorite book and try to write a new ending. It won't happen overnight, but maybe it doesn’t need to.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

“There is a moral of all human tales: 'Tis but the same rehearsal of the past, First Freedom, and then Glory; when that fails, Wealth, Vice, Corruption, barbarism at last. And History, with all her volumes vast, Hath but one page.” ― Lord Byron
I enjoy swimming in the ocean.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I love Byron and all, but I find this perspective kind of depressing, can't lie. It's like saying nothing ever changes, and we just keep going in circles. But don’t you think that’s a bit too pessimistic, or elitist? If you look closely through history, you’ll find tons of little progress quirks embedded in these seemingly endless cycles. Civil rights, women's right to vote, climbing out of deeply entrenched injustices, freedom of expression—all these didn’t exist when Byron was around! I mean, history isn't just a single page where everything stays the same. We’ve made a lot of progress. Sure, there's backtracking sometimes, but that's more like personality lines than one straight storyline. Just thinking about what’s going on today, I feel like we do have more pages being written, each more complex, crazy and riveting. Then again, history should be more than a linear progression, There’s a good conversation to be had about what values each society gains and what they lose. I guess I’m just mulling over where we are on Byron’s "page" now.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

[Warhammer40k] What type of music would each faction in the Imperium of Man or even other factions like?
I tried asking R/AskScienceFiction this question but they removed it. I don't know why I wondered this, I just thought it would be funny seeing a faction listen to music you'd never think they'd listen to, like the Iron Fists listening to Lady Gaga.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh, this is a fun one! Warhammer 40k factions with their own taste in music is a wild thought, but totally entertaining. If I had to guess, like, okay, take the Space Marines, for example: I think most of them would probably be into, like, epic orchestral music. It matches their whole larger-than-life, stern vibe. But then again, you have chapters like the Space Wolves, who might dig something more raw and energetic, like Nordic metal. Think guitar riffs that are as intense as a fight with Orks. Now, the Imperial Guard? I can see them leaning into military marches or something that helps them keep morale high while dealing with endless waves of enemies. Steel drums, maybe, or something with a drumline to keep everyone on beat. For the Adeptus Mechanicus, it's got to be techno or industrial. They’re all about machines, so it only seems fitting they'd appreciate music that’s all about electronic sounds and beats that could almost mimic their mechanical hearts. And then you've got factions like the Chaos Space Marines. I feel like those guys might like something pretty chaotic and intense. Maybe some hardcore metal or experimental sounds that are as unpredictable as they are. The Eldar? They’d probably be into something really sophisticated and ethereal. Kind of like ambient space music that's as intricate and grand as their crafts and aesthetics. Finally, the Orks have probably got a love for something upbeat and chaotic, like punk rock. Just banging and screeching, kind of like them. They’d love something loud and rebellious, matching their nature perfectly. Figuring out a musical match for each faction could go on forever. Imagining a Tau grooving to synthwave or Necrons vibing with darkwave... well, it could give those grimdark future battles a whole new background beat...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What if Reddit got rid of post and comment voting?
No more orange and blue arrows



They receive the following reply to their post:

Wouldn’t that be the wildest thing? I kinda think it would be chaos, which could be awesome or a disaster. Suddenly, everyone’s on equal footing and popular opinions wouldn’t be the default winners. Trolls would probably have a field day, right? The upvote system keeps some semblance of order, or at least a societal signal of what’s valued in a thread. Without it, Reddit might turn into an endless stream of mindless chatter or, worse, the echo chamber could implode. Either way, it'd be like the Wild West of opinions. Not sure if society is ready for that.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

A small step in the right direction is still a step in the right direction
Anti consumption can be an overwhelming concept for a lot of people. Corporations have spent a lot of time and energy conflating spending money with happiness and breaking out of that mindset is understandably a struggle. With this in mind it’s important to remember any sustainable choice makes the world a more sustainable place. You might not feel you can go vegan but you might be able to eat a meal with no meat once a week. You might not be able to start an allotment but you might be able to start a herb garden. You might not be able to boycott Amazon completely but you might be able to check local businesses for products first. There will always be more you could be doing and that can feel hopeless however doing something is always better than doing nothing.



They receive the following reply to their post:

cool.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Hardener tubes rotting for body filler type things
So I used to do a bit of home mechanic stuff which involved some rust ‘repairs’ and the tubes of hardener for body fillers ALWAYS like become brittle and start just decomposing for whatever reason End up with half a can of body filler with no hardener Same with wood filler/builders bog - tubes rot and perish I have to fill a couple holes where some screws tore out and I have to make a special trip to buy another can of stuff which I’ll use like 10% of and then put in the garage where the hardener tube will just degrade



They receive the following reply to their post:

Oh man, I feel you! This is one of those little, annoying things no one warns you about when you're doing DIY stuff. I went through this when I was trying to patch up a garden statue, and let me tell you, finding that crumbly mess when you go back for more is beyond frustrating. One thing I’ve started doing is storing the tubes in a ziplock bag with the air squeezed out, and then stashing them in a cooler, dry area rather than the humid garage. It’s not foolproof, but it’s seemed to help a bit with the shelf life. Once, I even put a couple of silica gel packs in the bag to keep moisture away. Honestly, though, sometimes I wonder if they design these things to just disintegrate so we have to keep buying more. Such a pain, especially when you just need to quickly fill a couple of holes. And those special trips to the store for one thing that you’ll only use a tiny bit of? Ugh, it’s the worst. I’ve heard from some folks they’ve tried storing them in the fridge, but I haven’t dared go that far yet. Wonder what my husband would say if he found car filler next to the yogurt...

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

Iwtl British accents.
I want to learn British accent, do you think it's something teachable?? Or you just learn by interacting?



They receive the following reply to their post:

I think you can definitely learn a British accent even if you think you're all thumbs with accents. But you need to know which one, 'cause there are loads of British accents, right? There's your classic posh one like the Queen's English or the modern RP, but then you’ve got the Cockney, Scottish, Scouse, Geordie, and so on. It’s like a whole world of accents over there. I remember when I was first trying to mimic the British accent, I was watching tons of British TV shows and listening to podcasts, just to get the rhythm and flow of it. Plus, there’s this thing called “shadowing” where you repeat words or phrases after hearing them—it helps a lot. Some people say practicing with a native can fast-track the process, but I didn’t have that luxury, so it’s not impossible without it.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

What's going on with long books right now?
There seems to be this attitude right now in this sub which I assume is perpetuating from the publishing industry itself that long books are a bad thing. It seems like anything over 100k words is simply inadvisable these days and not worth writing if traditional publication is in any way a goal. This is slowly driving me mad. Most of my favorite books are at least around the 200k word mark. Most anything I were to write would be deliberately shooting for that length. Like I'm sitting here reading first man in rome and I'm just thinking, this is amazing but according to this sub this should be literally unpunishable now. I just don't understand what's going on. I understand our population as a whole has had a decrease in average attention spans but it seems to me we're functionaly working in a handicapped medium if larger traditionally published works are simply impossible now unless your an already known author. Yes of course most books written at that length have substantial editing to be done before they're ready to be published but if you were to say write a 500k word novel no amount of editing is getting that down to 100k words while still in any way communicating the authors intent. It seems the same to me as the arbitrary 2 hour restriction Hollywood often has which often results in movies which could have been great if longer cut to shreds, so audiences don't get bored presumably. Advise often given here is to cut the slower stuff, make sure everything progresses the plot, essentially making sure absolutely nothing boring is on your page by the end of the editing process. If I compare that advise with my favorite novels however it seems nonsenseical. In many of them the slower sections are the point. Even something as mainstream as Tolkien's lotr is an incredibly slow book and I very much feel that's a huge part of the appeal. I feel like by limiting ourselves to certain lengths and by enforcing that we have to essentially bend over backwards to keep the audiences attention during that already short length with which we are left we are as writers inherently blocked off from writing in the format of longer, deliberately slower, more complex books which I find most compelling. I'm just curious how you all feel about this. Obviously no shade against the people telling others they need to make theirs books shorter to get published, it goes without saying that this isn't their choice and they are just communicating the requirements of the industry at this time.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I agree that long books seem like they’ve fallen out of favor, but I think a lot of it comes down to market pressure. Publishers want to hedge their bets and assume shorter books might be an easier sell, especially if they're dealing with new authors. The risk is lower if they print a 300-page book that doesn't sell well versus a 900-page behemoth. Plus, printing costs are a real thing. A bigger book means more paper, which means more money. But I'd encourage you not to be so discouraged. A lot of the longer genres, like epic fantasy, are still getting published, though it feels like they only greenlight wordy tomes if it’s part of a series (those can be intimidating too, come to think of it). I’ve spent more time this year checking out books on different self-publishing platforms—and let me tell you—there’s plenty of room there for longer works. A friend of mine wrote this massive fantasy epic. He decided to self-publish because he wanted to keep control of the story and not have to cut it down to fit a corporate officer’s checklist. He found his own audience by just posting online and sharing with other fantasy fans. It takes some work, but it seems he has connected with readers who value length and complexity. I wonder if we’ll see a shift in traditional publishing, maybe they’ll start to embrace the longer format again. Until then, hang in there. When you find those readers who live for the details and complexities, the slower burns, those are your tribe. I guess there's a little bright side in the self-publishing path, not needing to fit into anyone's word-count box. But anyway, yeah, this topic's been swirling in my brain too.

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

People who say "let people enjoy things" when someone complains about something.
I was looking a music sub a frequent, and a user made a post saying he wishes people would stop spamming the sub with their Spotify Wrappeds. The entire comment section was just people saying some variation of "it is what it is" or "let people enjoy things". Its like people cant comprehend that maybe you want to express frustration with something.



They receive the following reply to their post:

I get where you're coming from. Sometimes, it's just nice to vent a little when something's annoying, and it feels like you're being shut down if every response is just, "let people enjoy things." It can feel like no one’s listening or taking your side seriously. But I think people say that because they're just trying to keep the good vibes going, you know? It's not that they don't understand the frustration. Maybe they're just not into hashing out the negatity. In my experience, trying to phrase it in an enjoyable or fun way can make a difference. I used to get all riled up about the constant barrage of pumpkin spice everything come fall. Like, we get it, the pumpkins have arrived! One year, I turned it into this whole silly thing where I’d just talk about how every store was being “attacked” by pumpkins. That led to some laughs and less stress about a trivial thing. I guess people like to see joy because it keeps them from thinking of all their own frustrations. Sometimes, though, just going to that other corner of the internet (even just for 5 minutes) that vibes with what you're feeling can help blow off steam without all the "it is what it is" chorus raining down.

They receive the following reply to their post:

You know, I’m not sure I totally see the need for yet another platform like this. I'm always a bit skeptical when new tools pop up that seem to do what a bunch of others are already doing. I’ve seen folks get pretty comfortable and efficient using existing sites like Wix or Canva for landing pages. Plus, for managing tasks and timelines, tools like Trello or Notion have been doing a bang-up job for a while now. Maybe instead of trying to get people to shift to a whole new platform, it could be beneficial to see how those existing platforms get people attracted to their services and why people keep going back. I’m all for new innovations, but sometimes it’s just easier to stick with what people already know. I’d be interested, though, if your platform does something really different from the usual. Just a thought, maybe as more people try it, you can see what extra features they like better.

They receive the following reply to their post:

This right here is the magic system equivalent of when you’ve got a big puzzle, but you’ve just tipped the entire box onto the table and now you’re staring at all the pieces wondering where to even begin. But honestly, the details you’re sharing sound pretty fascinating! I’ve dabbled in creating a magic system myself, and it’s like trying to staple Jell-O to a wall sometimes. You know, all gooey and you’re never quite sure if it’ll stay up. One thing that really helped me was to pick one central concept or rule that everything else hangs off of. You’ve got a lot of concepts here with the source network and different types of sources—maybe focusing on one, like the source networks being akin to a nervous system for magic, could tighten things up a bit. It might give you a framework that everything else can logically stem from. When I was developing mine, I started with a concept that magic was like radio waves. You can manipulate them but you need the right technology, or in this case, magical tools or skills. It helped me figure out the limitations and consequences of using magic, which turned out to be key in making the system feel grounded. Your potions idea is cool! It kinda turns the usual “here’s a mystical brew” on its head 'cause you’ve got these efficient source-infused pills instead. Finding how to weave these neat ideas into your broader world could be the way forward. It’s like, let the world evolve naturally around the magical stuff you love most. Maybe those pills tie into daily life or culture in your world? I’ve always found that weaving magic into the social fabric can give it depth and make it feel integral to the world. Anyway, you’ve clearly got something unique going here—don’t let it intimidate you. Maybe even step back, shove it into a drawer for a bit, and come back with fresh eyes. Ideas tend to marinate well when you forget about them for a while. Yeah… those are just some thoughts to chew on…

A user makes the following post on a social media site:

How do I switch from PR to Advertising?
This seems dumb, but I'm currently a public relations student who realized that advertising and marketing would be a better fit than PR. I don't love doing press releases or anything like crisis management, and I'm more into media strategy, graphic design, and brand strategy. However, I'm too far in my degree plan to switch majors now. How do I successfully land more advertising jobs and internships as a PR major, and what skills should I specifically highlight to get those roles? Or what do people recommend for navigating this switch? Also, let me know if there are any certifications that employers like versus what's useless.



They receive the following reply to their post:

Honestly, switching from PR to advertising isn't that huge of a leap. Many of the skills overlap, which can work as an advantage for you. Focus on the skills you've already got that align with advertising, like your knack for media strategy. That's big. And hey, graphic design and brand strategy are super in-demand. Try to work on a portfolio that showcases your design and branding chops. This could be mock-up projects or case studies, even if they're not 'real.' In the ad world, showing what you can do speaks louder than fancy degrees. Maybe take online courses in platforms like Coursera or LinkedIn Learning—many of them are highly regarded and don't take much time to complete. I'd look into courses about digital marketing strategies since digital is everywhere now. Internships or entry-level roles in agencies are a great step. Oh, I remember when I did my first solo trip without supervision when I was around that age—it was such a big deal! First, I'd say show your parents that you are on top of things with a solid plan. Maybe sit down with them and walk through the details so they know you’ve thought it all through. Give them a clear itinerary, let them know where you'll be staying, and show them that you know the area, like any campgrounds or landmarks nearby. Safety is a big point, so make sure to have an emergency plan. Pack a first-aid kit, bring plenty of water, and don't forget to tell them you have the necessary gear and enough food to last your trip, plus some extras. And have a reliable way to communicate, whether it’s a phone, map, or GPS. Maybe you can even download offline maps in case you lose service. And then, show them why this trip is important to you, like how it’ll help you become more responsible and independent. Parents usually love hearing that these experiences are great for personal growth. If there's a way to check in with them throughout the trip, that might ease their minds too. Tell them when you’ll call or text, and keep those promises. Plus, make sure your friends’ parents are a part of the convo too. Maybe if your parents hear from them, it’ll help them see the bigger picture. You’ve got this, and I’m sure they’ll come around once they see how prepared you are.
